extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, scientists, and educators interested in principles of evidence, eyewitness reliability, and higher-education standards
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the reliability and scientific value of human testimony and observer-derived evidence, and related commentary on educational standards for scientific instruction. Emphasizes cognitive/psychological limits on observation and implications for legal/scientific evidence and for designing college courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability of testimony from trance/entrancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony of those who are even partially entranced or in trance is of no value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trance is an entirely subjective state (external causes only excitants); a person in trance may do things contrary to their will, experience hallucinations of sight/hearing/other senses, and persist in delusions after the event. Therefore testimony from entranced persons should be treated as scientifically worthless. The author reports experiments (e.g., simulated magnetization, professed cures, staged ‘ghost’ performances) showing many persons can be induced to experience nonexistent phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of emotional excitation and psychical contagion on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When emotions are strongly excited in a group, psychical contagion spreads excitement and renders concurrence of testimony unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crowd multiplies emotional response (likened to an electrical machine where each revolution adds force); under such conditions a whole audience can simultaneously see or hear things that do not exist. Examples: mass laughter or tears at performances, simultaneous relief of symptoms in staged experiments. Under strong excitation the number of witnesses does not increase reliability — 'a million ciphers are worth no more than a single cipher.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses alone give no certain evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses of themselves can give us no evidence of anything whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools, courts, and writers commonly treat the evidence of the senses as unquestionable; the author argues that, because of brain limitations and involuntary mental processes, sensory reports are not self-authenticating and must be critically examined in light of psychological factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention/volition can impair observation; good observers observe without conscious strain
rubrics_metrics.description: The very effort of attention is liable to destroy the scientific value of observation; a good observer can observe without severe, conscious effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and examples: Lynch and Goethe on productive states where one is 'in a state rather than making an effort.' Attention may subtract cerebral force from faculties needed for careful attention. Only when observation occurs without forced volition can it be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty is an insufficient primary qualification of a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing honesty as the first qualification of a witness is erroneous; honesty does not protect against involuntary error produced by emotions or brain states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., Esser cited approvingly by others) assume honest witnesses are more trustworthy; the author counters that honest witnesses may sincerely hold false convictions resulting from wishful thinking, emotional influence, or involuntary mental processes, so honesty alone should not be decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized observation skill (expertise) matters more than general intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: General intelligence should not be conflated with special intelligence; expertise and trained observational skill are essential to reliable testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and standard practice often treat general intelligence or the form of swearing as sufficient to make testimony valuable; the author argues that swearing cannot make a non-expert into an expert. Example: microscopists not yet experts often 'see what they are looking for' and later believe they observed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrence and number of witnesses are not definitive guarantees of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement among numerous witnesses does not necessarily make testimony convincing or incontrovertible, especially where concert, contagion, or emotional excitation is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classical maxims (Laplace, Abercrombie) that improbability plus concurrence implies truth are critiqued; experiments and psychological phenomena show numerous similarly-entranced witnesses can concur in delusion. The possibility of simultaneous deception via contagion must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony about marvelous or unprecedented phenomena has particularly low scientific value
rubrics_metrics.description: Average testimony concerning unprecedented, marvelous, or wondrous phenomena (e.g., supposed new forces, raising of the dead, unusual natural appearances) is of little or no scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phenomena strongly excite emotions of awe, wonder, reverence, or fear in large assemblies, increasing susceptibility to mass delusion. The author emphasizes that these are precisely the situations in which evidence is most needed yet least reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to reconstruct principles of evidence to account for involuntary mental life
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing principles of evidence (as taught by legal and philosophical authorities) must be reconstructed to incorporate knowledge about involuntary mental action and brain limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current systems wrongly presuppose senses and honesty as primary safeguards. A reformed evidentiary science should recognize unconscious mental action, the limits of volition, susceptibility to trance and contagion, and the difference between general and special intelligence. Legal forms (oaths, courtroom procedures) may be the best practicable but cannot correct cognitive limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges should employ faculty with appropriate specialized training
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects should be taught by instructors with special, up-to-date training in the discipline (e.g., modern philology for classics; scientifically trained teachers for the sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes institutions where classics are taught by mere grammarians and sciences by teachers without special training. Proper scientific instruction requires teachers with real scientific competence rather than amateurs or generalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should not overclaim status or confer unearned degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: If an institution cannot perform college-level work honestly, it should not call itself a college or grant diplomas; it should take the name corresponding to its actual function (academy, high school).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many low-grade institutions damage the reputation of genuine colleges by claiming college status and awarding degrees to students who have not received genuine higher education; renaming and refraining from granting diplomas would be a corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid designing artificially easy curricula to attract poorly prepared students
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating easier courses or 'scientific' curricula primarily to swell student numbers undermines educational standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition for student enrollment encourages colleges to lower admission and graduation requirements, create parallel but easier curricula, and produce 'waste-heaps' of low-quality college work. Scientific courses should be clearly defined and rigorous rather than diluted concessions to popular demand.
